A review? I can't. I don't even know where to start. There is SO MUCH what I love about it, it's blowing my mind. It's like as if I took everything what I loved in life and put it into one game. Are you serious, Marko? 

Puzzles are engaging and feel very fresh, graphics are really cute and feel inspired, levels are just great through and through, I just love the design. Movement feels so nice, so smooth and I only get confused sometimes because I'm trying to push it to the limits, and it stands perfectly. 

And then there is music. No, I'm not talking about the fact that combat is rhythm-based, or the OSTs (which I've bought thank you very much). It's just that... EVERYTHING is so musical. Everything moves to the rhythm, connecting all elements into one melody. Sounds are never anoying or non-existent, they grab the attention where you want it but never take away all the space. 

And everything is just so... dreamy. Surreal. And you can walk there, and like in dreams, despite not making any sense, at the same time, it does?? It's consistent, purposeful, and so fucking beautiful. 

I love all of it. Would pay you several times if I could. Thank you!

Leaving a positive review for the game to continue supporting indie game projects, but this one definitely has it's issues.

Combat with trash mobs feels like a chore at times. There's not really clear telegraphing on whether or not you can make progress in certain areas leading you to feel like you clear up to 50% of an area and then have to turn around again.

The music outside of the boss rooms is 'very' repetitive and droning to the point where I had to turn it down outside of the bosses because it would seriously start to drive me insane during the puzzle rooms. 

Level design is chaotic, and I feel less like I can actively search for secrets so much as I just so happen to stumble into them because I misread the map at some point. There's some clear inspiration taken from Pseudoregalia, but the game is lacking a fundamental understanding of what made it fun to a slightly frustrating degree. 

If you can look past it's flaws there are some nice ideas here, and it's worth the asking price, but it is rough around the edges.

My problem with the game is the combat. It's extremely basic rhythm-game stuff based [b]entirely[/b] on doing the correct button presses at the [b]exact[/b] right time; enemy attacks and projectiles do not give a quarter ounce of urine how fast you're doing and will track your position expertly so you [b]have[/b] to engage them via matching the beat and little else. This is especially annoying when I want to just travel through a tunnel I've already been through and enemy skulls will fire homing fireballs at me and I just want to run on by but they keep scratching me fierce.

That aside, my bigger problem with the combat is that it doesn't make the most of the unique abilities and gravity of the game. You get some nifty tools to use and the fact that the game is just expecting you to have to match dodges and parries with the enemy feels rather disappointing, especially when the puzzles actually do make the most of your kit.

I don't like metroidvanias and I get lost easily, but I really like Metro Gravity. The rhythm-flavoured combat lends some freshness to the formula, never mind the fact that the 3D platform almost never has a strict up or down, which can be frustrating for someone like me with an awful sense of direction, but goodness if it isn't interesting!

Heavy focus on exploration and puzzle solving with a light sprinkling of rhythm-based combat wrapped in a low-poly, chill-vibed Escherian world. Metroid Prime style map that rotates with the camera so you can actually find what direction you want to go in, which is always nice but even more important since there's no total reference direction. Takes a bit of getting used to the controls and things are a bit finicky but when it works it works well, and the music somehow manages not to get old when you're spending an hour listening to the same track while you explore these areas and wrack your brain to figure out the puzzles, then an enemy shows up and you've internalized the rhythm without realizing it and you smoothly transition into combat mode. The combat is largely just "hit the right button when the circle closes in", it's just enough to break up the pacing without needing a whole lot of dedication to learning mechanics, obviously not the main focus or draw of the game, but not an unwelcome change of pace every now and again. Wonderful experience for anyone who loves exploration and puzzles and can handle a bit of timing challenge.

the gameplay is really fun and interesting and all the items do something to iterate on the gameplay in intuitive and enjoyable ways, especially since a lot of them have more than one inherent feature.

some of the puzzles are either really frustrating or just straight up don't work the way they're probably intended to, but the vast majority of this game's puzzles are really satisfying and make sense, they almost always play upon the idea of gravity very well. i also like that sometimes you can solve the puzzles in more than one way, and they'll sometimes throw something at you that seems complicated until you take a step back and think about it in a simpler way.

probably my favorite part of the game is the environmental design. the way you get introduced to each new area sometimes in a piecemeal fashion only to come there for real a second time is a good quality for a metroidvania to have, and the map itself is interconnected in a really cool fashion that makes it feel really dense and explorable. it really nails that 'getting lost in the halls' feeling that i think the dev was aiming for. as for the areas themselves, they're all really creative and interesting, with each of them having an operative gimmick that usually relates to whatever item you pick up in that respective area, though i would argue that quite a few of them could've been iterated on and made longer, like the aqueducts and the red desert. 

without question, metro gravity's weakest point is its combat. i don't even necessarily mind the rhythm elements (especially in regards to some of the bosses) but the trash mobs in the overworld are pretty grating, more or less acting as bullet sponges that stall for time and give nothing in the way of rewards for defeating them.

i think the music was cool, and i really enjoyed how everything the player does (from attacking, to walking, and even parrying) ends up aligning with the background music. it's like one step beyond a dynamic arrangement to where it almost feels like you're playing to the beat of the song rather than the song is reacting around you which is honestly a highlight of the game for me.

overall like 8.5/10. does a lot of really impressive stuff, but can be kind of tedious and frustrating at times. wish it was longer and maybe the story was a little more climactic and interconnected, but the game doesn't overstay its welcome and is thoroughly enjoyable for the most part

Important: Definitely play the demo first to get a feel for it as this game is NOT for everyone, but if it's for you then it's REALLY for you.

Things that I loved that are noteable:
-This game's movement and systems will be mind-bending for a while, but it's extremely satisfying to figure out and get into a flow that works for you. 
-The story and presentation are very solid, especially for how short the game is I found myself really enjoying the characters, atmosphere, world, and writing.
-As someone who plays a LOT of games, it consistently surprised me with how many unique ideas it has both with it's gameplay and quality of life features.

My main negative is the combat. It's not very intuitive or as satisfying as other similar games, and the first boss at the end of the demo seemed waaaaaay too difficult. Fighting normal enemies also felt like a slog, they're annoyingly persistent and can often attack you at a much higher range than you're expecting, because of that I tried to avoid them whenever I could. 
BUT as you progress you get more tools to help avoid normal enemies. Bosses also get better since they become easier as you go, and they're much more fun to look at than actually fight (other than maybe the final boss and the boss you fight on the beach, they're both great). 

Lastly: you get the best item in the game after the first boss, so if you beat him in the demo and have fun swinging around like Spiderman, then things are only going to be better from there and I'd highly recommend buying the game!

Definitely an experience that will stick with me for a while, can't wait for you to make more games!!

This game is a great visual experience with some mind bending 3D layouts as you're allowed to walk on almost any surface and change gravity through a few abilities. I love the aesthetics of the game with it's low poly look, the character designs, and the music adds a great ethereal vibe to it all.

However, while I do recommend others to try this game out, I have a two very frustrating gripes with the game. And I apologize for my harsh tone.

1) During combat the game is rhythm based. Whenever you get into combat a little combat metronome appears in the bottom right of the screen. You can ignore the rhythm, however the enemies will base their attacks on this rhythm, and you will deal more damage if you attack on the beats. However this visual metronome is so tiny the visual barely helps at all, it might be better somewhat near the middle of the screen but more transparent. But worst of all, the timing is quite tight for dodging attacks, and at the same tight super fast. During the second enemy I found the best strategy was to spam attacks before the enemy could even attack. Now granted this could be because I suck at the rhythm, but I feel like the game's combat timing is way too fast and hard for the start of the game. [spoiler]I also encountered the first boss... which is completely rhythm based, you aren't even required to do damage. Which makes my cheese strat of rushing damage useless. Just outlast the song that plays while dodging at very precise times with attack patterns you have no way of predicting until your 4th or 5th time. [/spoiler]

2) The puzzle designs. The puzzles are quite elaborate at times and quite difficult. I thought I had stumbled into a bonus area and was doing a puzzle where I had to protect a flower from three flame throwers using a block. Now when I first entered this room, the flower was moving down its rail automatically, but when trying to move the block around somehow the flower stopped moving on it's own. This made the puzzle maybe impossible. I spent around 20 minutes trying to figure this puzzle out until I left the room, and came back later. I found the flower was moving again and tried the puzzle again, which worked first try. And then I realized the puzzle was mandatory. Which comes back to my main point, the puzzles feel quite difficult for being just at the start of the game. I thought I was getting a broken heart collectible or something, but instead this is intended as the main path. And each puzzle I've encountered has had some quirk that was frustrating in some way.

My main gripe with the game is that the game feels like I've jumped into it halfway or more into it. I feel like there should be a tutorial, or slow ease into the mechanics, where the game has thrown me into the deep end.

I don't like writing such a critical review on an indie game like this, because I do really enjoy the aesthetics and world this game is offering. However while playing I feel annoyed by the combat and some of the puzzle layouts, which ultimately leave me with a negative perception of the game.

But overall I think others may enjoy it more than me, so I still recommend it on steam. But with some caveats.

What I received was a game frankly too big for it's britches and too difficult for me to justify giving it more of my time. I think if you took one or two of these concepts out to hone in on some of the others the game would be, frankly, perfect. as it is I feel like the game is decent at best and agonizingly frustrating at it's worst.

The artistry and skill on demonstration here are top fucking notch and frankly I'd rather have 100 of these kinds of games out there than the next AAA release. The character design, music and level design are fucking fantastic. I cannot stress enough just how many of my issues are nitpicks that prevent me personally from enjoying both this game specifically and games in this genre. Puzzle platformers, metroidvanias, and souls like games are all extremely not up my alley. I think I was smitten by the gorgeous art style I didn't pause to consider how much I would be basically trying three genres all at once that I don't normally touch.

And, hey, who knows. Maybe I'll come back to this game and appreciate it for what it is: A wonderful title oozing charm and skill out of every crevice. But for now? It may be time for a refund

I played up to the first boss so far as of writing this review. There were some positives and some negatives, but overall I had a good experience. Movement feels a bit slow and floaty, but once you get access to the gravity beam (which you get quite early on), you can use that to traverse which makes exploring much better. How the gravity changes based on where you are standing + the gravity beam is an excellent combination and it works well.

The game is filled with tons of puzzles, which are well made, and they stay fresh. In the first chapter, there were block sliding puzzles, physics puzzles, etc. The harder ones have hints available for people (like me) who aren't very good at them. But I found them enjoyable and not too difficult.

Aside from the boss fight, fighting normal enemies doesn't really feel like you are "on beat" like advertised. Rarely did I actually parry or dodge to the beat, because I found it much more effective to just walk outside of their attack range, and spam attack to kill. That being said, the music was fantastic, especially for the boss fight. The main exploration sections have a relaxing jazzy feel to it, then for the boss it really upped the energy with a kind of metal vibe. The boss was by far the best part of the game, and I cant wait to see more of them.

Overall, as a solo developer's first game, who made it in his spare time after school, in about a year, this was pretty good. And the price is very reasonable.

After having played the demo previously, I can only say that there's nothing quite like this. Rhythmic combat with parrying? Mind-bending environments that do not fall (no pun intended) under standard laws of physics? I'm all for it.

I was expecting a mixture of Mario Galaxy and Gravity Rush, and I got that. I wasn't expecting Portal-like puzzle rooms, or how the game turns into a more freeform Hi-Fi Rush whenever you enter combat because of how central the beat is to enemy attack and movement patterns.

And yet it doesn't feel like any of those games specifically because of how unique the combination feels.

I guess the best way to describe it is that I went in with a certain expectation, then had to repeatedly change that expectation as the different components of the game revealed themselves. This lead to some frustration earlier on, but after a while I realized that I needed to let go of those expectations and meet the game on its own terms. At that point it started to click in place for me what Metro Gravity is trying to do.

The game can roughly be divided into four different gameplay loops:
1. Mario Galaxy/Gravity Rush-style platforming.
2. Portal-esque puzzles where you have to apply your avaiable tools within a limited 3D space.
3. Rhythmic battles with enemies like Hi-Fi Rush (the bosses especially are big spectacles with a lot of countering and dodging that has to happen on the beat of the music).

If I have one criticism, it's that it is often a bit unclear what you're supposed to do next, but thanks to the map you can usually figure out where to go.

Other than that this game is a very unique blend and I strongly recommend checking it out if you're a fan of crazy platforming or big puzzle rooms, with the side note that you also need to enjoy or at the least be able to tolerate rhythmic combat because you will be doing a lot of that.

Metro Gravity is a short 3D Metroidvania in an old school polygonal 3D graphics art style. The gameplay consists primarily of two elements: Puzzle solving and Fighting. Both complement each other nicely such that the gameplay never beecomes to dry from the puzzling aspects or too intense from the fighting aspects. This is tied together by the core gameplay mechanic of manipulating gravity - your personal gravity is at all time the last object you stood on.

The puzzles are good and a couple had me stumped for a bit until I figured out the solution. Combined with the exploration innate in a metroidvania, you often will backtrack to old areas where you can now solve new puzzles with new mechanics.
The fighting system is rhythm-based and at times feels more like a parry-based rhythm-game. You have to parry the enemies blows according the the timing and right parrying method and in the 'off-beats' you can attack yourself. It feels fresh and fun.

In summary, this game felt unique and interesting to me and didn't disappoint me in any aspect. The gameplay is fun, the art is gorgeous and even the writing it funny. I recommend it to people liking metroidvania with interesting gameplay mechanics such as e.g. Animal Well.

Insanely good. While Metro Gravity wears its inspirations on its sleeve (Gravity Rush, Pseudoregalia, Sekiro, Portal...), every part of the game glows with such bold imagination that it quickly establishes a fresh identity and becomes something truly unique as it develops. I just finished the game and absolutely loved it.

The art and tech are outstanding. It runs beautifully on Steam Deck. The world design is dizzying in both its complexity and its cohesion. Some of the environments are jaw-dropping.

As a big Sekiro fan, I found the combat extremely enjoyable. It takes rhythm parrying to a new level, lining up enemy attacks to whatever track is playing — and there is so much music! I love that the player benefits from familiarity with each song.

I'm not a puzzle person, and I looked up the first couple solutions online, but as I played through the game and unlocked more abilities, I began to understand the language of its systems, and I surprised myself by solving some tricky puzzles just for some collectibles, or for the thrill of figuring it out. I still can't believe it, but solving some of the harder puzzles were among my favorite moments.

And wow, there are some real MOMENTS in this game, some authored and some natural. A heavy line of dialogue, a private note that sinks your stomach, a badass animation from Stephanie when you pull off a crazy stunt, a wicked character design, a bizarre new enemy, a shockingly cool new phase of a boss, entering a new zone with colors you feel like you've never seen before — it just keeps happening, moments of surprise and delight all the way through the end of the game.

I feel like I could go on and on, but I'll conclude here with a succinct bit of praise: Metro Gravity breathes new life into great ideas to achieve something special, compelling, and gorgeous. Thank you, mrkogamedev, and congratulations on your incredible first game.

This game is one of the most unique 3d platformers I've played in recent memory. To me, it feels like a game meant exactly for me. The gravity mechanics, alongside the [spoiler] grappling hook [/spoiler] results in a movement system that, after you get used to it, is maybe one of my favorites for it's high potential for speed and depth. The rhythm combat is tough, even as a musician, but it's incredibly satisfying to finally get that weird rhythm some enemies and bosses throw at you. And, of course, the soundtrack is just fantastic, especially in the boss fights that combine all of the above. This game weaponizes the musical prowess of the dev, so get used to seeing that "Maybe Next Time...". Especially if you're not used to the syncopation, tuplets, and odd time signatures the game will throw at you. I will say though, unless you REALLY do not take motion sickness well (which is a very valid complaint, the camera struggles to cooperate at times), at the very least try the demo. You will not regret it. This is one of my new favorite games, hands down. I haven't even mentioned the characters and exploration. I found the characters to be very fun to talk to, and the lore goes fairly deep (also worth mentioning the amount of references to real life musicians, it's very funny sometimes) . And exploring the map (while confusing at times due to the nature of a 3d map without any consistent sense of what is "down") never gets old, as you get new tools to solve puzzles (which quickly get difficult), open shortcuts, and find new ways to speed through the rooms [spoiler]The grappling hook in particular is maybe one of the most fun things put in a 3d platformer[/spoiler]. If any of that sounds fun to you, I suggest you try it out, and tell a friend to check it out too. This game deserves far more attention. Also, if you are crazy about music theory like I am, this game will still exceed your expectations. 
To summarize: this game is very, very, very good. It cuts no corners for any of it's mechanics (though that does leave them a little rough around the edges), and commits to them entirely. And this is one of those soundtracks that comes with a free game. I still can't believe that this was made by one developer. Try the demo first if you're skeptical, but make sure you have that $12.99 ready afterwards.

The title tells you pretty much what to expect lol. Metro Gravity takes Pseudoregalia's approach to adapting metroidvania elements to three dimensions as a starting point but takes those foundational ideas in a whole different direction, with slower paced exploration based around exploring every wall and surface in every room looking for new paths and secrets paired with difficult puzzles, which is occasionally broken up by rhythm-like combat sections. I enjoyed playing this game for the most part but there were a lot of things that felt frustrating about it.

Exploration in a world where you can walk on any surface seems like it would be hard to pull off but it's actually done very well in Metro Gravity. Rooms are designed in such a way that there are no primary surfaces and a lot of pathways branching out in all directions, with the map being very interconnected. Impressively enough the map is also fairly easy to interpret despite the world having no up or down. Most of your movement abilities are given to you early on as well so you have plenty of time to master them and explore where you wish. Unfortunately the game's movement always has a halting feel to it even after you've unlocked every ability, as there are few abilities that let you move really fast and those that do tend to only work in specific areas or tend to end up in you running into obstacles and sticking to them, having your whole camera shaken in the process.

The game's structure itself starts out fairly linear until reaching the first boss after which you have the abilities to explore largely at your own leisure. The areas you explore are visually diverse, with Red Desert and Gambler's Palace being standouts, and are packed with collectibles; in my own playthrough, I think I found less than half of them. The areas tend to all follow the same trend though of having a central hub with beams of light/chains/whatever leading out to X number of hands/torches/weird rocks that you have to destroy/activate/light to open a door or whatever in the main hub. This meant that whenever I was frustrated or annoyed with a puzzle or wanted to explore something new, all the other areas available to me had largely more of the same to offer which was disappointing. Enemies all have interesting designs, but there isn't any benefit to fighting them and whenever you pass one, the camera locks onto it and forces you to go towards it (and when you manually remove your camera from it, it often locks on AGAIN, or to the enemy's neighbor) which is super frustrating to deal with while passing through old areas.

I didn't enjoy the puzzles much. While they tend to involve interesting uses of the gravity mechanic in moving cubes or other objects around, most of them share the same problem in which the solution to a puzzle is obvious but hard to actually pull off because you're fighting the controls or camera the whole way. There are SO many puzzles in this game where you have to manipulate the gravity of a cube multiple times in mid air to make it land on a VERY precise spot, having to start over if it diverges even slightly; or spend a minute setting up the puzzle environment to open a second-long interval to get whatever's locked behind the puzzle; or, worst of all, puzzles where you have to manipulate one object to clear the path for another, but the game's camera only lets you look at ONE of these objects at a given time so you are basically in the dark. Well at least they ended.

The boss fights are probably the greatest spectacle in the game but the hardest parts as well. They are basically rhythm sections where you have to parry each of the boss's attacks to the beat, or based on the indicator superimposed on the boss, until they tire out. Attacking is optional and there are only rare movement-based challenges that break up this rhythm. While the music and visuals were interesting, the attacks from the boss don't correlate well with the music and the visual indicators are rather weak, especially when the boss is attacking a lot at once, so beating a boss fight can feel like a process of trial and error memorizing the attack patterns exactly as they occur - in a typical rhythm game you'd be able to see the notes yet to come but you get no advance notice in Metro Gravity so changes in a boss's attack patterns often come by surprise, or with a green indicator which doesn't give a whole much information. In general, there is a sense in Metro Gravity that the rhythm elements and the actual gravity elements are two separate things - they tend to occur independently of each other in-game and involve separate skillsets, and nearly all of your progression goes towards the latter. It would be interesting if these elements were integrated more closely.

My favorite part of Metro Gravity's visual style is the vibrant colors everywhere - each area has its own signature color scheme and it's cool to see them blend into the blackness of space that surrounds the map. There isn't a strong underlying theme to any of the character or enemy designs; they seem like whatever the developer thought was cool, and they are cool to be fair. The story is similarly all over the place in terms of mood and is a bit complicated. The characters are all interesting though even if you don't spend much time with any of them. One gripe I had with the game's art direction is that the animations on the whole feel very stiff, as though the characters were all action figures. Enemies' attacks seem limp, which has the effect of making them harder to read and react to, as well as reducing the drama of boss fights and the sense of motion while exploring. 

In retrospect it's amazing to think that a game like Metro Gravity blending so many seeming discordant elements and ideas can turn out working as well as it does, and in light of that boldness it's easy to forgive a lot of the flaws present. Metro Gravity is fresh, inventive, and just plain different from other games and I feel there's a lot of value in playing a game like this that reminds you how cool the idea of walking on walls is and how cool it is to be able to do that in a video game, and that we can even do things like that in video games.

I will say getting as many hearts as possible and giving it patience will reward you, you'll feel like a task is impossible but after giving it time so you can learn it you can overcome it. The bosses patterns are set, so you can memorise them! I don't think this is a negative for the game but the more casual of gamers beware it just might not be for you.
Lastly, if you have some trouble with motion sickness in games this game is a stomach churner, you will be doing flips and weaving around through every direction gravity can take you, and it could be sickening for the weak of stomach! But for the Gravity Rush fans, you won't be disappointed, this game also gives you roller coaster butterflies all the time.

Ok onto the actual review for Metro Gravity.

I've been following this game since around the beta came out sometime last year, and even with how promising and fun that demo was the game outdid itself from then with perhaps 4 times more content on top of that demo. 
The music is always absolutely amazing, the vibes are fun and exciting, the visuals are interesting and creative, it's an absolute feast for the senses. You get a great balance of chill exploration, brain melting puzzles, and engaging rhythm based combat.

On the topic of music, every part of this game is completely centred around the music. Your footsteps are synced to the beat, Stephanie will bob her head and tap her hand and foot, holding out an ability it will swing in your hand with the sounds on beat, and all of the combat and rhythm puzzles are on beat too. It's always intuitive to interact with when everything is synced up this way and is endlessly satisfying, like while you're playing you also get to be apart of the jam and part of the music itself.
Every area's theme is a great mix up so you don't feel like it's all same-y and it doesn't get too repetitive, a good comparison is how in Deltarune/Undertale some songs can be relatively short and loop but I can listen to them all day. You might find after playing this game some of the songs getting stuck in your head, and they make excellent themes to play in the background of your mind. 

The world of Metro Gravity doesn't have an up and down, and not just the world but pretty much every single room and location isn't defined to a specific up and down. You're encouraged to look up and down and make complete use of the space you're in. For exploration it means it's easy to miss stuff, but running back through an area can often be a completely fresh perspective. Throw one of the several abilities that can be used for mobility into the mix and you can be pretty creative and free with how you navigate the world. This is a huge plus for a metroidvania that *will* have you going back through the world to look for stuff either for the collectables or to progress.
One aspect that can be hard to wrap your head around with no real up or down, is navigating in the literal sense. Where have you been and where are you going? Luckily the in-game map is a huge resource that makes navigation much easier. You can move the map around and rotate it, you can view a full world map to contextualise where areas connect, and you can place waypoints although the game places some really handy ones already for you (such as elevator locations, save points, npcs, and what area a part of the map leads to next).

Puzzles are HARD. Well, some are. Some puzzles will be an absolute breeze and it's just a matter of getting your bearings and clicking the right spots with your abilities. But sometimes? You will actively feel like there's no WAY you're intended to solve a puzzle the way you did, and yet there's no way else to do it. It really does have some creative out of the box solutions, so make full use of your mind to solve them, take risks doing something you don't think should work and you'll feel like a genius for doing stuff that other games might make you feel dumb for trying.
It really is portal tier puzzle design, sometimes they're real easy but some will feel impossible and they require some very clever use of your tools (or in some cases, un-use? Like, undoing a tool effect). If you're really stumped, some puzzles come with a handy phonecall to your pal Oscar for hints, and he'll try to be helpful without solving it for you, so don't feel ashamed to ask him for a tip! Or, worst case scenario, ask the community either in discord or online, as they're always happy to lend a hand!

Combat is secondary to the music, and as a system is entirely reliant on it. It's satisfying and fun, but don't expect sekiro or nier out of the combat, it's a rhythm game. It's mostly about timing your parries on beat and getting in attacks when you can. Parries are not on the same type of timing as games like dark souls or sekiro, you really are incentivized to parry ON BEAT and not just before, and the game does tell you that but it's easy to miss. It's honestly pretty generous at times, where you will look like you full on got hit and you still get the parry, but it's also really easy to trip yourself up and parry too soon which makes the cooldown to parry again sometimes too long to get it off in time.
You can parry faster than you'd think, spamming it out of combat or off-beat will be rather slow but if you block an attack you can essentially parry again right away. Combat doesn't have much depth past parrying and clicking attack when you can, but it doesn't need more depth it's not the point of the game, and it's already pretty difficult at times.
A small tip, bosses don't need to be attacked at all during the song, just parried, attacking is just for score!

The last thing to note about this game is certainly not the least, as it's the story and characters. Some of the characters in this game are absolutely adorable and fun (Domǐtǐlle my bestǐe~!) and even the ones that might seem like dicks, like Sinatra or Ms Davis, are troubled but chill and good people. You will not regret getting every collectable to get a great post-game treat.
Along with the fun dialogue from this colourful cast you can find documents littered about with lore implications and story relating to the 'outside' (the real world). Most of these documents are rather depressing, the game is so cheery that the depressing undertones hit pretty hard. All of these characters are stuck here for reasons relating to some personal trauma or issues, and sometimes it's a pretty serious topic. Even the bosses are just people that have been stuck there for an unfathomable amount of time for some sad and terrific reasons.
The final fight for me was the easiest skill-challenge wise, but man it mighta been the hardest just for the implications to the story. It's a real trip.

Again I cannot recommend this game enough, the experience will not leave you with this game, it's a game I won't be forgetting along with other classic indies such as Pseudoregalia, FTL: Faster than Light, or Risk of Rain. And as of this review it's CRIMINALLY UNDERPLAYED. This game deserves to blow up! The one man team, mrkogamedev himself, is surely up to some amazing projects in the future, he even has some really interesting gamedev blogs that are entertaining and informative both for people who are interested in game design and people developing games, check him out!

Really amazing game. The developer has put lots of thought into making the experience as good as possible.

The main unique feature is the gravity switching mechanic. It makes traversal and exploration feel very unique. It can take quite a bit of getting used to, and some people will definitely not be okay with it - but is really cool and makes for great moments and scenes. There's also a button to lock your current gravity direction, which is a small addition but is so convenient - you can focus on fights, avoid sticking to walls and lets you choose not to interact with the gravity switching if you don't want to.

Traversal in general is enjoyable, and doesn't get tedious - this is great for a Metroidvania. There's multiple other mechanics which make the travelling convenient. The 3D layout of the halls make places seem complex, but things are never that far away from a fast-travel point.

Combat is tied to the music - it's quite basic, but there's ways to cheese this if rhythm isn't your thing. After the mid-game, you can find enough health to tank damage without needing to play the rhythm game at all. There's also items which let you travel so fast you can skip roaming encounters. The choice to let you defeat bosses without attacking is genius - this also lets you focus more on the music.

The puzzles weren't too complicated, but there were nice ideas and aha moments every now and again. Most puzzles aren't required to beat the game, and many of the difficult ones let you optionally get hints.

There's not even much roughness. The entire experience is just really, really good. It knows what it is, and doesn't pretend to be more.

Absolute masterpiece of a game. Took me about 12 hours to 100% complete, which is incredible playtime for a solo dev project that isn't a roguelike. 

Puzzles are really rewarding and difficult, and there are really good hints and solutions if you're an idiot like me who can waste ten minutes trying to force a solution that doesn't work. 
Combat is personally one of my favorites, it mixes Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice with rhythm elements that make every enemy (even the ones I hate **** you record player guy) totally fair with no room for argument. The bosses are probably the best part of the game, immaculate set design, spectacle, and difficulty. I never had a hard time with the bosses after learning their moveset, but they certainly aren't easy. The cherry on top is the genius way of adding your own difficulty through a points system, where attacking the boss is completely optional, but weaving attacks with your defense gives you points that you can see in the menu. 

Another reason the bosses, and by extension the whole game, is amazing is the music. The dev did an amazing job making the soundtrack, and there is not a single bad song to be found. It also leads into the rhythm mechanics, which are done really well. A metronome on the bottom right of the screen tells you the tempo, and following the tempo of the area you're in is necessary if you want to avoid getting bodied.
The movement is the most hit-or-miss part of this game. Many call it janky, and while I think that's fair to say it doesn't quite give it the justice it deserves. It's hard to get used to, it is incredibly disorienting, and it feels so amazing when you get used to it. I'm not even close to being good at the movement, but even then I still love pulling off stunts with the tools it gives you, and it deserves recognition for being so good despite the difficulty of making this function.

Each area is unique, and the game in general has an amazing aesthetic that never wore thin. Though since you so easily get lost, and the gravity mechanic is very annoying when you aren't used to it, the gameplay loop would get tiring very quickly if you're used to non-stop action.

The story is the last thing I'll touch on. The story is very strange, and it relies heavily on putting puzzle pieces together, almost like a mystery you're solving. If you don't engage in stories, this won't be special in any way, but if you really try to engage by reading every document and talking to all of the characters it shapes into something that's best left for you to find out yourself. 

TLDR: Amazing combat, bosses, music, and visuals. Really good story. movement, puzzles, and progression. Don't play if you get annoyed easily because it will make you angry.

Metro Gravity is a super slick gravity puzzler / rhythm game from an incredibly talented solo dev that I had a blast playing through.  It was really hard choosing how best to order the positives this time around because I feel like all the systems are equally important to fulfilling the vibe the game is going for and it wouldn’t be the same if they weren’t all present.  That said, I need to get this review out there because I desperately want more people to find Metro Gravity, so I’m just going to wing it.

[h1]Positives[/h1]
([b]+++++[/b]) [i]Everything you’d want to see in a warped gravity world is there.[/i]  From long, twisting hallways to water falling at odd angles and buildings sprouting from the tops and bottoms of rooms.  You even get to experience that classic localized gravity on planet-like spheres.

([b]++++[/b]) [i]Needle & Thread.[/i]  I’ll be honest, I didn’t realize the Needle & Thread acted as a grappling hook when I first got it.  I knew of its uses for puzzles but it didn’t occur to me I could zip around the map utilizing it until a while later.  But when I did, oh boy could I just not stop using it.  In a game with a bunch of nifty tools, the Needle & Thread is by far the most enjoyable.  The momentum in this game is top notch!

([b]+++[/b]) [i]Puzzles![/i]  As someone who greatly enjoys puzzle solving in a 3D world, Metro Gravity features some pretty stellar puzzles that could only come about due to the game's mechanics. 

([b]++[/b]) [i]Boppin’ Beats.[/i]  This game has a jammin’ soundtrack that lays its influence throughout the journey, so much so that even your character walks on beat.  This point also segways nicely into the section:

([b]+[/b]) [i]Boss Battles.[/i]  Truly the highlight of the combat system.  They feel like playing a song map in a standard rhythm game with the added twist of weaving in your own flourishes to the dance and I enjoyed each one immensely.

[h1]Negatives[/h1]
([b]--[/b]) [i]Motion Sickness.[/i]  Honestly, probably the biggest complaint I can muster.  The character and camera can take a little getting used to when they’re constantly rotating about the room and I know I personally almost gave up on the game when I had to shut it off after about thirty minutes.  Luckily, this game has a fantastic demo that allows you to see if the movement sits right with you.  If you get a headache then you don’t need to go through a refund process.  Then,  if you like what you played, full game progress picks up where you left off in the demo.  Very cool! 

([b]-[/b]) [i]Not Stylin', maybe Profilin'.[/i]  [strike]Not even a complaint really, but I wish outfits you unlocked in one save could be used when you go back in for the speedrun achievements.  I understand why it doesn’t work like this, but I think it’d be cool :)[/strike] As of the most recent update, 1.1, outfits unlocked can be used in new save files, as well as some other speedrunning QoL, so this qualm is mute.

[hr][/hr]
	Now here’s a new little section for me: [b]Mixed[/b].  Some things that I thought were good but I didn’t fully vibe with for one reason or another.  Think of it as feedback, I suppose.
  
[h1]Mixed[/h1]
[h3]Map[/h3] 
(+) Clever idea to have the map turn with your camera, so the area you’re aiming for on the map will be where your character is facing.  Extremely useful navigation tool.

(-) I wish you could put waypoints at areas you want to go to, not just where you currently are.  It is quite easy to get turned around or lose the spot you were going for when you accidentally rotate the map as you cling onto a new surface.  It’s a learned skill I suppose but it would’ve been helpful my first go around.
[h3] Boss High Scores[/h3] 
([b]+[/b]) Getting more parries gives you a higher multiplier for any hits you work into the dance, which is a very cool way to incentivize parries without forcing them.

([b]+[/b]) I like how you have to weave in your attacks during the fight to get a higher scorer, meaning you need to learn the fight inside and out.  

([b]-[/b]) You can’t just press a button to reset a boss you messed up on, you need to either Save & Quit or let the boss defeat you.

([b]-[/b]) [strike]Wish you could challenge bosses from a menu instead of needing to go back to their room first.  All elevators can take you back to bosses you’ve already defeated, granted, it just takes a little extra time.[/strike]
EDIT: With every update, more and more of my qualms are rendered obsolete.

I *tentatively* recommend this game if you have a lot of patience for utter bullshit, or you don't have *any* intention of doing side content. I had fun playing it, up to a point. However; this game really should be advertised as a puzzle game primarily before a metroidvania or a rhythm game; it *features* elements of those genres, but outside of boss fights and the extremely limited ability unlocks (there are only three items that actually unlock new progression outside of keys, and imo keys don't count) the core and bulk of the experience is a puzzle platformer, especially if you want to do any of the side content which is almost entirely puzzles.

The rhythm-based combat is fun and interesting, if very shallow, the gravity-control platforming is fun, if sometimes nauseating and clunky. The majority of the mandatory puzzles for story progression were fun and fairly intuitive to solve (except for one, which I swear is either bugged or *incredibly* jank). The game sometimes has issues signposting when you can actually solve a puzzle or if you are missing an item to solve it, and in the mid game it can be particularly hard to track progress-blocking items down, but the progression through the story was overall fun and worth experiencing. 

However, I cannot say the same if you want to do all of the side content and go for 100%. A number of the puzzles require such precision and speed that they were impossible for me on a controller, requiring switching to Mouse + Keyboard. A lot of the puzzles are also just extremely frustrating to figure out and then solve even when you know the solution: some have extremely specific solutions that require you to intuit very niche mechanics used only for that puzzle, some are just super jank and it feels like they take dozens of attempts to make them "work" to give you the solution (basically every single momentum-based block sliding puzzle, which were nearly universally super fiddly and imprecise), and some require a frankly absurd amount of speed and timing for how utterly janky the control scheme of this game is. Having to change gravity direction multiple times consecutively with how finicky and imprecise the gravity control is was not fun, at all.

I had fun with this game overall; usually when I play a metroidvania I try to complete as much side content as possible. With this one, I decided to try and get 100% after beating the final boss but am putting it down at around 85% completion to save my sanity.

If you are going for just the main story and the bulk of the content of the game, I would probably give this a 7 or 8 out of 10. My opinion plummeted when I started going for 100% and experiencing some of worst the game had to offer.

Metro Gravity is a really weird and charming 3D metroidvania which, like its name implies, revolves around gravity.
Right from the start, I was shocked when I realized how much effort the developer put into that mechanic. You can walk everywhere: on the ground, on walls, on the ceiling, even on random everyday objects. The gravity shifts everytime you approach a different surface. It was quite disorienting sometimes, with the camera having to constantly reposition itself 😄
It's extremely impressive that it was made by one person. It must have been a nightmare to code all of this.

The game feels very dreamlike, firstly because of the story, but also because of a few other things: the low poly artstyle; the cryptic dialogues; the boss arenas feeling very out of place; and the world design being reminiscent of Escher's Relativity (think of that picture with all the stairs upside down going in every direction).
Sometimes you'll also stumble on isolated rooms with small planetoids floating in the void, a la Mario Galaxy. It was so peculiar, but I enjoyed it a lot. All in all, this is a perfect playground for a game that toys with gravity!

The combat relies heavyly on parries, and the boss fights are like rhythm minigames. You don't have to attack during those fights, just deflect every hit. There are also bosses that rely more on parkour and the use of your gravity items, these ones were a lot more fun.
If you decide to play the game, I just want to let you know that you can increase the parry window in the settings. I thought the timing for the parries was pretty tough, but fortunately the developer gave that escape route for the players who don't want to deal with sweaty combat.

The items & abilities you get are really fun. Several of them are physics-based: for example you have a needle to [spoiler]attach objects together[/spoiler], and a [spoiler]gravity beam similar to Portal 2 to move an object from point A to point B[/spoiler], plus a very satisfying grappling hook! On top of that, there are more traditional MV abilities like a dash, a double jump, and a dive.

I struggled to figure out some mechanics and puzzles on a few occasions, but overall it was a very fun trip.

Metro Gravity is like straight drugs to me. The combination of Legend of Zelda inspired dungeons and a unique movement system created one of my new favorite indie games. It has its imperfections but I was easily able to overlook them considering all of the cool things Metro Gravity does. Personally, I put this game up there with other indie titles like Signalis.

(The OST is also really good)

I want to start off by stating that I don’t normally write reviews for games. But the sheer level of creativity and passion on display here is too much to not comment on. Metro Gravity is a 3d platformer/metroidvania with three gameplay features which set it apart from other attempts at these genres, gravity switching, puzzles and rhythmic combat. An odd blend of genres and gameplay mechanics which sound like they shouldn’t work together, there’s already a pretty low number of 3d metroidvania titles indicating that it’s a genre that’s difficult to get right on it’s own. So how does MG fare with more genres than your average triple AAA title? Extremely well. 

Gravity switching lends itself to puzzles quite well, you’re character also finds a few other tools which feel like they’ve been utilized in these puzzles to their fullest extent. The puzzles themselves have been well designed and there’s not a single bad one here. Okay that’s a lie, there’s three. But three bad puzzles in a sea of good ones is a stellar accomplishment. It helps that the puzzles I have problems with, all have optional rewards behind their completion, none are required to make progress in the main areas. 

As mentioned, the game's combat is rhythmic. In Metro Gravity that means the rate which an enemy attacks is dependant on the tempo of what song's playing at the time. Foe's in this game can attack you from a distance meaning you'll be blocking attacks frequently and attacking inbetween. Sometimes you'll be trapped in rooms with a tough enemy, you can't just spam the attack button as you don't have enough health to tank the damage. As a result these battles feel less like a battle for survival and more like something akin to a dance. (A comparison which the game humorhously points out at several points.) The bosses are an exception to this however. More on that later.

The game fully embraces the metroidvania style. At the start, while you're adjusting to the gravity mechanics the developer's careful not to throw too much at you for the first few areas. Once the first boss is defeated the game really opens up, allowing you to tackle any of the three other bosses in your own order with minimal backtracking involved. Speaking of, backtracking is a breeze. Most of the areas has at least one warp point and gives you a map of the area pretty early on. Usually you'll only be backtracking for optional collectables which the game has quite a few of, including items you can give to the side characters for extra stuff.

Now's a good time to talk about the story, I wont spoil any major plot threads so this section will be light. The main character, Stephanie has no memory of why she's in such a nonsensical place so it's up to her to fill in the missing gaps by learning why everyone else is here. Stephanie and the side characters are very well written with plenty of world building and collectable notes which flesh out the game's lore a bit. However if you're not here for the story you won't be bored, apart from some dialogue and some cutscenes the game's story takes a back seat.  The world building and lore are optional. 

I don't have much to say on the soundtrack. I'm not a audiophile but I did find the ost very enjoyable to listen to, so much that I even paid to get the soundtrack on Steam.  If you like Jazz with some chiptunes sprinkled in, you won't be disappointed. 

Alright, coming back to what I mentioned about the bosses. Make no mistake, they're well designed, and they adhere to the rules of the combat. But the first one in particular is a difficulty spike. Other games would garner some criticism for this but with Metro Gravity it's difficult to fault it. Only two things change with bosses, the frequency of the attacks you need to block increases. But instead of a health bar, the length of the boss is tied to the length of the sountrack. When the song ends, you win. It's undeniably challenging to get used to, but I'd recommend putting on some headphones so you can clearly hear each beat, that's helped me with timing blocks.      
Aside from that, difficulty isn't an issue here but if you're really struggling with some bosses there is an 'extended parry option' should you require it.

The gaming landscape is in a bit of a weird spot right now. I know it, you know it, our wallets have felt it for years. But indie games like this, which aren't afraid to take risks, remind us of why this hobby is awesome. Despite it being the developer's first big game, it feels like they've been working in this space for years. Their passion for their ideas really shines through and I'm excited to see what they'll come up with next. All this considered, I think Metro Gravity is an amazing experience and well worth your time and the cost of entry.

As someone who gets motion sick, I found that the gravity locking mechanic and setting camera smoothing as fast as possible helped a lot.

For anyone planning to buy the game, I would advise thoroughly looking around each room, checking all the walls before moving on. I found that I once misses a mandatory path because I didn't look up in a room and didn't see the giant pathway there.

To conclude my thoughts, this game does everything great, even if there are some drawbacks that come with the nature of it. The environments are beautiful and varied, the boss fights are cinematic, the puzzles all use the gravity mechanics and tools to be interesting, the story is unique, the music is stunning, and (most importantly for me) the movement is smooth and fun to play around with. I recommend.

A wonderful and unique platformer that you really ought to give a whirl if there's any love in your heart for 3D platforming and physics-based puzzles.  I played this one with a game pad and it felt great.

The core mechanic is of course the subjective and malleable gravity.  Touch a surface and you'll "stick" to it standing upright, that surface becoming your new "down".  If you jump, you fall back in that direction.  For example, you could step out of the front door of your house, walk up the the wall and onto the side of the building, jog a pace or two and jump off, to then fall down your street to get to the grocery at the end of the block quickly, then walk through the top of the door frame and along the ceiling to get to the milk section in the back, bypassing the aisles and people on the floor.  It'd be a sweet power to have.  Mercifully, there is no fall damage.  You really have to open your mind to the possibilities but you might find it starts clicking surprisingly quickly, for how alien it is to the real world.

You get plenty of powers that alter things further, such as locking your "down" to whatever it is currently, a directional dash usable in the air, a double jump, projecting a field on a distant surface to set anything "above" it to treat that surface as "down", a lasso that you can use to pull things towards one another, or swing around like Spiderman, a remote rotation tool and a rapid downward stomp.  Things like the gravity field and lasso especially also affect enemies so beyond puzzle solving, you can use them for creative combat maneuvers.

The puzzles are fantastic.  They make good use of the mechanics and really force you to think according to the physics of the world as well as how to use your powers to accomplish what you need.  That includes working timing and momentum, so there is a skill aspect to it beyond simply figuring out what to do.  They require enough thought and practice to be satisfying when you complete them, without any crossing that line to become too frustrating, at least in my opinion.  The hardest ones are optional, of course.

Combat is a weak point, in my opinion.  It's all rhythm-based, but the ambient music is fairly chill so when an enemy gets in combat range and slips into that tempo, it really doesn't feel as connected as it should or sets out to.  Fortunately, there are ample visual cues to accompany the auditory ones, so I found myself relying upon those.  Attack range is generous and the attacks themselves automatically track, so you don't have to worry much about non-timing precision.  Helpful given the odd environments and gravity shenanigans.

Bosses are an exception, since they have their own tracks and are more of a set piece, allowing them to match the music far better and more obviously.  You don't actually have to fight the bosses either, you just have to survive the dramatic display until the end.  You can attack for points, but they don't really matter, so timing the parries and dodges to the often quite aggressive barrage of attacks is all you really have to focus on.  It feels pretty weird but the system works.  The first boss especially will feel like a substantial difficulty spike, so look out for that.

The characters are pretty cool and the protagonist, Stephanie especially is relatable and likable.  You have to work to get the most of the story, as the world is a strange place and many of the conversations or lore bits are hidden as puzzle rewards.  It's good stuff if you put in the effort though.  The graphics have a low-poly and simple texture style, with pixel art for portraits.  I happen to like it and it fits the very abstract nature of the setting but if you're looking at the trailer and dislike it, know that it's representative.

Even if the rhythm aspects don't sound like your jam, I encourage giving it a try to experience the very well-executed gravity mechanics.  There's a demo so you can try before you buy, but the price is certainly reasonable, even without a sale.

I will say spacing matters and with enemy attacks pushing you when you parry and your own attacks moving you forward as you swing sometimes you just end up in a weird position and attacks hit you even if your parry timing is "correct" to the beat just cause you're standing in a weird spot for the hitbox. There was one later game enemy that every time I fought it I would always miss the 3rd block on its swings if I was standing too close. So not perfect, but not bad.

The real star of the show for me though was the boss fights. The first boss really sets the tone of how they go with a kick ass soundtrack that comes in hard and fast compared to the otherwise kind of chill overworld music. The boss fights are pure rhythm game; timing dashes, jumps, and parries to the beat of the music. Attack windows are sparse but also more a bonus than anything else as hits only add score until you've reached the "end" of the fight and the boss finally gets a small healthbar to smack through to finish them off after they've exhausted themselves with their onslaught of attacks. Each fight is a wild spectacle and worth the full ride of the game.

The game's puzzles are also pretty good with some of them actually requiring some intuitive out of the box thinking that you don't often get to see in games. Even just figuring out some of the interactions needed to progress the story takes a bit of thought and nothing is so painfully obvious that it's boring while also avoiding being so much of a headscratcher that you give up. Hits a solid balance.

The story... I feel takes a backseat to the gameplay. There is some interesting ideas and some good world building in here, and there is definitely a point to everything and a consistent theme throughout; but it's not going to knock your socks off. There is some depth and thought for sure. And it was interesting finding the bits and pieces that built out the world. I also enjoyed the side characters and all their little interactions and quirks. None of them have insane in depth fetch quests or huge meaningful story arcs but they're not completely static either. Just memorable enough for me to have a favorite of the cast for their little bit of story and design both. Nobody fell into the background as completely unmemorable and without note which can be hard to pull off with some of these kind of games.

Metro Gravity is a rather difficult game to summarize. If I had to try to wrap all of its elements up into a single statement, it would be a puzzle platformer with gravity shifting mechanics, a rhythm combat aspect, and light Metroidvania progression. Simply reading that might have one thinking "that's a lot of hats to wear at once" and it is, and it's all being juggled by a one-man dev team at that. Throw in a contrast between its whimsically dreamlike environments and the darker undercurrent of its characters and narrative and "ambitious" is a word that certainly comes to mind with this game. Honestly, I think few will love every element of this game equally. It's not so much that any one part is a drag on the others - it speaks to the developer's talents and passion that everything here in isolation actually works very well. And yet, once you spend a few hours with the game it all comes impressively close to gelling together. I'm not sure if I'd say it quite pulls it off, but Metro Gravity has an audacity to it that few games really go for nowadays and that's truly commendable.

There's a multitude of perspectives to be had with this game given that it tries to do as much as it does, but I can only really speak sincerely from mine as someone who enjoys games like Gravity Rush, Pseudoregalia and Super Mario Galaxy. Upfront, this game had me at "gravity-shifting 3D Metroidvania" and if we stop right there, the game is a success.  I loved tinkering around with the main tools for exploration and the level design mostly leans into taking advantage of the 3D space and perspective without being too overbearing. That said, loss of orientation is pretty much inherent to this concept on paper and Metro Gravity not only doesn't escape it, but almost seems to lean into it. I liked this aspect of the game a lot, but for those who have difficulty navigating 3D environments normally or just don't enjoy getting lost, this aspect of the game will probably be rather annoying - you ARE going to get turned around in this game.

And then there's the rest of the game, which all needs to be taken in the context of this being a gravity-shifting 3D Metroidvania, a concept where it's already challenging enough just to maintain your bearings. Starting with the rhythm-based, parry-heavy combat, this is a mixed bag in execution. On one hand, the range of your attacks and putting enemy attack patterns on a beat does somewhat offset the awkwardness of fighting while shifting perspectives (though you can also just lock your gravity down as well to help some). On the other hand, said shifting can make it very difficult to even learn enemy patterns in the first place, and I found myself taking a few game overs from focusing so much on learning an enemy pattern that I accidentally walk into a wall, have the camera shift dramatically and completely lose my bearings and rhythm in the process. This is less of an issue with boss fights, which mostly dispense with the exploration tools and focus more on more intense rhythm patterns, but not only do these feel like trial and error as you pretty much have to feel their patterns out in real time but they feel like they come from a different game entirely. Those who do a better job intuiting the game's audiovisual cues might find these parts to be the most fun across the entire game, but it begs the question of what it really has to do with the 80% of the game that isn't a rhythm game.

The puzzle elements are much more in line with the Metroidvania concept but simply put, Metro Gravity's puzzles are no joke. It's one thing that you'll always need to be mindful of looking at a puzzle room from literally any angle, but there's a lot of times where the intended solution or mechanical use case isn't conveyed as clearly as it could be. I probably solved about 70% of these puzzles on my own, but sometimes I'd look up a walkthrough after bashing my head in against a puzzle for over an hour because I could see steps 1-4 and 6-10, but for the life of me couldn't figure out step 5. This extends to some of the basic item gating as well, there is some very esoteric use of your items and sometimes I'd walk away from a room I could enter just because I didn't know how to open the door, even though I had what I needed to do so. Those coming in from a game like Pseudoregalia hoping for another 3D Metroidvania should bear in mind - this game is less about movement and much more about puzzle solving, and I do think there's a little too much reliance on sheer player intuition to just read the developer's mind on what they were going for. That said, those who love mulling over a good puzzle will certainly find some here.

So, do I recommend Metro Gravity? Yes, but not as emphatically as I hoped I would. This is very much the kind of game where one can love a third of what's going on here to death, but then slog through the other two-thirds just to get more of the parts they love. And make no mistake, I adored parts of this game. I had my share of frustrations, but I was charmed enough to see things through to the end. That aside, there truly is something respectable about a single person determining to make a game of this scale and ambition, actually following through with it, and coming through with a product that is exceptionally competent by that metric. The game truly is the kind of effort that I want to see succeed, if not see more of. I wholeheartedly recommend the demo as it's a big enough vertical slice of the game to see if this mixture of ideas is something that's up your alley. Overall, I think Metro Gravity can be difficult to love in its entirety, but it has something that most everyone can love about it.

Metro gravity is so many things: a metroidvania, a rhythm game, a puzzle game. Those different layers are blended together seamlessly. The parts of the game that left the biggest impressions on me were the Gravity, the Soundtrack, the Bosses, and the Story.

The Gravity.
There is no up or down in this game. Think Super Mario Galaxy. Paired with the abstract level design, this leads to a somewhat confusing, head-spinning, but undoubtedly unique, interesting, and enjoyable experience.

The Soundtrack.
The games score ranges from tranquil, to upbeat, to adrenaline building, and they just don't miss. I'll speak more to it in the Bosses section, but the boss tracks are all absolute bangers. Multiple songs from this game have made it into my regular playlists, they're that good.

The Bosses.
The Bosses are where the rhythmic core of Metro gravity shines the brightest. Every boss follows a pattern set to the tune of the music, and every attack is played in time with a percussion, key, or guitar riff. Additionally, there's a score meter and combo multiplier, score being gained by landing attacks, while your combo is raised as you successfully deflect incoming attacks, or lowered when getting hit. In my opinion, these factors make for some of the most cinematic, heart racing boss fights I have ever seen in a game.

The Story.
The Story follows your character, a young woman named Stephanie, who is a witch with the power to control gravity. The lore is delivered to you in short & sweet dialogues with charming characters who know only a bit more than you do, as well as having their own perspectives about the world around them, with notes and documents which hold a surprising depth of information. Nothing is spelled out for you plainly though, it's up to you to piece together what all of it means.

As a closing statement, it's rare that a game is so good that I not only /want/ to 100% a game and it's achievements, but also see it through. Metro gravity has it's hooks in me. This game is a monumentally creative endeavor from a devoted solo dev, and it has quickly become one of my favorite indie games of all time and I cannot recommend it highly enough.

This game has two very different elements to it, which are largely separate. They coexist together without friction, but they also scarcely interact so I want to talk about them separately
[h3]Gravity-Bending Metroidvania[/h3]
There are a handful of games that play with gravity in one way or another. In select few you can walk on any surface, making the walls and ceiling your new floor. Very, very few take this concept as far as Metro Gravity, where not only can you gravitate to [u][b]any[/b][/u] surface — be it ceiling, tree, or upside-down beach umbrella — the maps are also designed with a complete lack of downwards direction. A floor of one room transitions into wall of another, all oriented in a large and interconnected space. By default the map will only show you the current biome, which helps in you not getting too lost since each biome is relatively small on its own.

However, as far as metroidvania maps go, it is on the simpler side. It is hellishly difficulty to make a good 3D map where down can be any direction, so the same things that help you not get lost make the map a bit more streamlined than one might want. There is still routing you can do to go your own way, but the new movement tools you get tend to feel a lot more like keys for particular doors than tools that suddenly open up the map through a bouquet of little shortcuts all over the map. They are generally very useful though.
[h3]With Rhythm Combat (and bosses)[/h3]
Throughout the world there are enemies scattered about, both small and large. There is a good variety, but aside of ones that you need to defeat to unlock a gate they're inconsequential, with little to no reward for killing them. It's a shame cause the combat could be a lot more expanded and involved. The tools used for metroidvania traversal could be integrated into combat, such as [spoiler]disarming foes with the needle,smashing into them for damage/armor break with the heavy disc, or revealing weakpoints on an otherwise undamageable enemy.[/spoiler] A lot of potential to integrate tools from the other half of the game into this one that isn't quite realized.

What is very well realized though, is the boss fights. Trying to dish out as many attacks as you can, while parrying the incoming attacks, while avoiding unparryable attacks with dashes and jumps; all to the rhythm? Absolute peak. They're dances of death, but it's up to you who's the grim reaper. They're also the main source of replayability, since the more attacks you want to squeeze in the more score you'll get, but the harder it'll be to execute.
[h3]And Some Rough Edges[/h3]
Finally, as I mentioned, this is a first-time solo project so it's not without some rougher parts. To start, there are some game design inconsistencies. Sometimes the rhythm combat timing circles appear on the enemy, sometimes on you. Walls of a specific color in the factory are movable by a mechanism, aside of a particular similarly-colored block that you have to move manually. Glass is usually just decoration, aside of the one time when it breaks. None of it is particularly bad, but it does stack up to paint the image of the developer not being seasoned in their craft. Which is perfectly okay, and I'm sure will disappear with future projects/patches.

There are some things people might enjoy less. While the music is generally good (though at times feels a bit quiet or completely disappears) the animations are... present. Some of the bigger moving things (e.g. bosses) are a bit jarring or too simple for their size and importance. There are some very cool set pieces and ideas across the bosses, but they can be undermined when the boss turns around by doing a 180 degree model rotation. Generally while the low-poly style is well executed (and warranted!), the animation and boss VFX are the weakest parts of the game


In the end, I had a lot of fun with the game. 10h to 100%, a little more if you want all achievements. But most importantly, a unique title if you're looking for something slightly different

This game is pretty fantastic. Its a 3D metroidvania that gives you a plethora of tools to direct you where to go, without feeling like you're being TOLD where to go or chasing a marker. Which is good, because this is a game where EVERY surface is walkable and there is no true right way up, you ARE liable to get lost (but in a good way). Movement can be methodical and paced if you want to take it slow, or you can full on Mario Galaxy and fall your way [spoiler] and grapple hook [/spoiler] around the world. Also got a Prime style 3D map which I mean... it practically necessary for a map to be useful in a game like this, but still rad to see. The game makes it so you automatically snap perpendicular to every surface you walk toward, land on, or dash into and it works really well. However there is a dedicated button to toggle it on and off, and there will be a myriad of situations where doing so gives the player a TON more movement option, so don't forget it if you're playing slower and then suddenly a challenge stumps you because you keep sticking to walls.

BUT, exploration isn't all this game has to offer. If you like Parrying and timed dodges, this games also going to scratch that itch. Along with a decently strong soundtrack, everything moves and attacks to the rhythm, including and especially the boss fights, which are filled with a mix of spectacle and endurance. Much like Sekiro, the game is built so players can really focus on defense, while also affording more skilled players to find more opportunities to attack.

And lastly, the puzzles. Not quite as numerous as expected. But, all the tools that make the movement fun also build into pretty novel physics puzzles that may leave you stumped every now and again. And in case you stumble on a CERTAIN physics based puzzle type involving a round object [spoiler] You don't just have to grapple the soccer balls to other points. If you jump and grapple the ball it will come to you. I felt SO mad at myself for waiting entirely too long to try that [/spoiler]

But to anyone who bought it or is playing the demo and are feeling iffy; trust the process, stay on rhythm (even if it initially seems like you don't have to, it helps YOU keep time if you don't mash attack), and get past the first major boss. Thats when you get the quality of life options you might be feeling like you're missing [spoiler] A compass and healing option [/spoiler], thats when schmovement happens, and its when it opens up more to a true metroidvania.

Dudes also been quashing bugs and tweaking QOL pretty quickly too, I don't know if he has people helping but thats some serious legwork.

Worth every penny.
