[h1]*Slaps Game* This Bad Boy Can Fit So Many Genres[/h1]

Out of all the moves your typical indie game employs to get one over the industry's big hitters, I think I'll always be most partial towards throwing a bunch of really cool, really stupid ideas at a wall and seeing what sticks. The kind of behaviour that sends a chill down any executive's spine, but the only kind that could possibly produce Metro Gravity, a wild amalgamation of puzzles, rhythm, parries, and massive boss battles all wrapped up in a metroidvania ribbon, and the only kind that could possibly make it as downright fantastic as it is. As the name implies, it's also deemed conventional gravity a little insipid for its liking because of course it has, and as that's really all there is truly permeating the whole experience, it’s as good a place to start as any.

[quote]For the best reading experience, please consider[url=https://summitreviews.biz/article/28/metro-gravity-review] checking out the review on the Summit Reviews website.[/url][/quote]

Simply put, down is always relative to the last surface touched; brush up against a wall and your feet will automatically flip up onto it, and attempting to stroll off a ledge won't see you plummet off but rather magnetise to its side as down is continuously redefined. Set in the otherworldly Halls, much of the environmental design is wholly adjusted to the temperamental physics, filling the space with corkscrewing corridors, tiny floating planets, and rooms with little regard for a definitive top or bottom.

A whole catalogue of excellent puzzles, too, equally in touch with the rules of the world, and impressing as a result of that understanding over any showy, ultra-advanced mechanics or convoluted solutions. Half of them are just moving-block puzzles when it comes down to it, yet these simple ideas are framed so differently and engage with space and directionality so unlike any other, you never really think of them as [i]just[/i] moving-block puzzles. It's a similar story with the metroidvania tools and trinkets facilitating each brainteaser; the first you find conjures up a sort of tractor beam, flipping the gravity of all that enters it towards its source, while another simply lets you tie and pull objects towards one another.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3539279132

Simplicity really is the name of the game here, but never to the point of triviality. Yes, you can describe each of your tools with a handful of words, but they're tremendously flexible as a result, and each new problem almost always comes with some new interaction or application. And sure, it's rarely hard to figure out what a puzzle wants from you, but there's often so much freedom in how you manage to bridge that gap. It's familiarity masterfully tempered with novelty—approachable building blocks brilliantly remixed in the flux of fickle gravity.

Solving a conundrum can be a somewhat disorienting task, however, and navigating the Halls even more so when up is down and left is right; yet, as tricky as it can be to plot a route, it's so quickly overshadowed by how utterly wonderful it is to simply move. Most of your puzzle-solving kit offers some form of unique movement tech—that tether doubles as [i]literally[/i] the best video game grappling hook I've ever used, to name just one—but traversal shines brightest as you surrender yourself to the new rulebook. You might walk through the first few corridors you find, but it really doesn't take long to realise you can just waltz up onto the adjacent wall and jump down the thing like a hole, and similar optimisations are [i]everywhere[/i] you look. There's so much freedom and self-expression in the movement, the physics and conserved momentum imbue it with such flow, and mastering the Halls' contorted geometry is genuinely the finest and most rewarding puzzle it has to offer.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3539279162

Metro Gravity is also *checks notes* a rhythm game all but through and through. From the cadence of your footsteps to even the pitch of the beep boops of conversation, the soundtrack dictates almost everything in the Halls, naturally extending to every facet of its relatively frequent combat encounters, too. Admittedly, calling it that is a bit of a misnomer; enemy attacks come accompanied with huge visual indicators very clearly prompting either a dodge, jump, or parry, your opposition rarely comes at you with more than one attack pattern, and your own strikes are just as bound to the music as your foes. It's certainly restrictive, but, again, this is a rhythm game, and combat very much fits that mould; each bout isn't so much a battle as it is a choreographed dance, and perfecting the routines of each of the Halls' denizens is a different kind of satisfaction altogether.

Nowhere is that more true than in the five major boss encounters, each oozing with spectacle and style, set to heavy, thumping tracks, and sporting far more advanced movesets to match. They're also even less of a typical fight, with no health bar, a set sequence of strikes, and only demanding that you simply survive until the end of the song to overcome them, your own attacks providing nothing but a slight increase to a somewhat bizarre and arbitrary scoring system. It works surprisingly well, however: while regular battles tend to expect a fairly specific sequence out of you, these bosses offer so much more control, and let you forge an encounter distinctly your own—it's never needed, but you very much get out of them what you put in.

Arguably more compelling is each of their backstories. To catch you up, you play as Stephanie, one of many who, following the completion of a dubious questionnaire online, find themselves stripped of their memories and spirited away to the Halls. Seconds in the real world stretch into years within, cruelly trapping its victims until—or if they even ever can—recall their final answer: a wish. One so profound and so desperate it transcends even memory. Steph's investigation takes her to the arenas of the Old Ones, as they're known, and alongside some optional notes you can later find, these monstrous locations warped and twisted by regrets their tenants can no longer even recognise are such remarkably nuanced and delicate, yet understated windows into their torturous existences.

Set to otherwise bright colours, upbeat music, charming characters, and casual, friendly dialogue, the juxtaposition is really quite effective. Battles rage through these massive manifestations of trauma, and all Steph can ever seem to think about is how much fun she’s having—this consistently dissonant, almost unnerving disposition always casting a tantalising shadow.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3542141725

I don't want to oversell the narrative; you'll spend a collective twenty minutes in conversation over the roughly eight-hour journey, even less time learning of the Halls' history, and the conclusion leaves a little to be desired, but it cultivates this unmistakable vibe—a sort of style guide that deftly holds all of this bombastic design together, and that really is the story of Metro Gravity. Created in its entirety by one Marko Popovic, it makes very little sense on paper. A puzzle metroidvania set in a world without strict gravitational rules is already a rich and diverse enough idea to fuel an entire game; throw in much more, and it feels as though you're beginning to muddy the waters. But if there's one thing that lets projects like this succeed, it's that singular vision of an equally singular person—development devoid of trepidatious outside influence or a fear to commit to its niche. It's the ingenious, ambitious work of someone creating exactly what they want to create and going at it with the sheer gumption to damn well pull it off.

I had high hopes from this game, seeing its gameplay and aesthetics.  Unfortunately I have too many gripes to stick with it.

The movement has a decently high skill ceiling, but feels too restrictive and clunky to properly appreciate.  
Minor obstructions and inconvenient angles make the gravity well unwieldy.  There also doesn't seem to be a nice way of removing a well that's in the way.  [spoiler]The grapple is a little unintuitive, but more pressingly is that the limited lampposts and small, restrictive passages mean I only feel the freedom of this ability when it is required.[/spoiler] It is also annoying and a little nauseating how the gravity can snap when walking over any little piece of geometry.  While I have no solution to the necessity of it, micromanaging the gravity lock is awfully tedious.

More than any of that though, the biggest mar on the game is its combat.  All combat in the game feels intrusive and lacking.  The flow of mashing attack and intermittently mashing block seems too simple on paper, and too clunky in practice.  Your own attacks feel poorly defined, with an unclear range and not enough feedback on hit, I mash the attack button until I've tickled the enemy to death.  Enemy attacks by comparison can be too brutal, juggling you and dealing more damage than I would expect.  Some enemies offer too little opening for how long they take to defeat, requiring 3+ blocks for every one safe attack.  And as combat grows more complex, it introduces new headaches.  The additional dodge types (dashing, jumping), while having generous windows, are reliant on the visual indicators which can often clip into geometry and become obscured.  Many of your abilities require aiming/looking elsewhere, so fights against enemies that benefit from these require giving openings where I cannot see their tells, which disincentivizes using my toolkit.  Some additional depth in the combat might help, but only if it is viable to use.  I did unlock a dash attack, which suggests there may be more down the road, but the skill seems kinda bad and I couldn't justify using it.  While the cinematics for the bosses are cool, unskippable cutscenes make difficult fights extra annoying.  Frequently the game could not bound my mouse, even in fullscreen, and would let me click outside the game; this has gotten me killed on several occasions.  And one of my biggest complaints is the way that any floating enemy has this tendency to circle around you endlessly, which caused a decent amount of nausea.

I hate to leave such a sour review, the game still has a lot of promise and is very impressive, especially from what I understand to be a solo dev.  Others may not have these issues or find them as impactful, but they are enough that I don't want to continue playing.

Wow the combat is bad.

It's infuriating before you understand what's happening, and it's deeply unpleasant after you figure it out. And the "aha!" moment of figuring out how the combat works? Also unenjoyable. It's like finding out a delicious looking dessert is full of a toxic ingredient.

This is a video game. Normally, in video games, what you see on the video screen, matters. That's why they call it a video game.

Not in this one, at least, not during the combat.

The sole determining factor in whether an enemy attack (projectile or melee) hits you, is if you pressed the correct dodge button during the correct time interval, or not. It doesn't matter if it it nailed you right in the face, visually. It doesn't matter if it went well to the side of you. It doesn't matter if you're still within range of an explosion or not, before/during/after the explosion. What's happening on screen is a complete decoy from the actual underlying mechanic, which is timing based, and given to you in audio (as well as small circles and a metronome on the HUD). 

At best, this is disorienting, and immersion breaking. At worst, it's downright jarring. The combat is asymmetrical: my attacks play by one set of rules (do they actually hit the enemy, and btw they're homing within a specific radius). The enemy attacks are playing by a totally different set of rules that have nothing to do with my rules. I'm having to play two non-intersecting games simultaneously. It's like chess-boxing if you had to play chess while boxing, instead of in alternating rounds.

Who on earth thought this was fun? When I played the demo, I immediately thought "well, I hope they fix the combat before the full release because what the heck was that?" Apparently, it's by design.

And the worst part is that the entire rest of this game is right up my alley. Huge winding corridors to explore, gravity mechanics, puzzles, the works. I thought this might be a good follow-up to Pseudoregalia. Turns out, the combat is so bad that it's genuinely not worth playing the rest of the game. And I'm not alone: 62% of players never beat the first boss (at least, I'm assuming that, from the achievements).

Play the demo, and if you like the combat, I'm sure the rest of the game is fantastic. If you don't like the combat: don't buy the full game.

[spoiler]Something about the courtyard after that first boss almost brought me to tears.[/spoiler] But I have a hard time recommending the game to anyone else. It has multiple issues that feel like they should not have survived playtesting:

[b]Motion sickness[/b]
====
Dear god, motion sickness. I love the concept of the game's movement, but the camera is -terrible- for it. The camera should not follow you nearly as much as it does. The player's focus point and sense of up and down is constantly shifting, and it's nauseating. I have VR legs, and I /still/ find this nauseating. It was getting to the point where I was closing my eyes whenever I walked onto a new "gravity plane." The camera system needs a wholesale rework.

I am writing this review instead of playing the game because I was getting too motion sick to continue.

A camera that does not get players motion sick should've been dev priority #1 with this game concept.


[b]Combat[/b]
===
The combat is just bad right now.

I think the concept is actually decent, though it risks feeling very "simon says" and lacks alternate approaches. But the execution lets it down on multiple fronts:
 
-Despite having the closing circle animation and the metronome to help, every single parry sequence must be memorized because there are effectively no other startup animations to cue the player. The closing circle often only indicates the first attack worth anything, as well; subsequent attacks often come too fast for it to be useful. I cranked SFX all the way up and turned the music down to learn the timings for the first boss, because the only reliable way for me to learn the attack rhythm was to hear it. I should not have to do this.

I would like to see bosses and enemies have animations that better telegraph their attacks; they honestly have no telegraph at all except the closing circle or dodge/jump warnings, it feels like, which feels lazy. But a more realistic ask that I think fits into the game—at least against the bosses—would be a literal rhythm game note scroll at the bottom of the screen indicating boss attack timings. That's basically what I'm doing anyways—playing a rhythm game.

Attacks are also bizarrely low contrast. The effects should be much more visible than they are. 

-The parry window feels unusually small for a game of this nature. I don't know if it actually is small, or if I feel like it's small because of the weak telegraphing and often quick parry sequences. And speaking of...

-Many parry sequences are too damn fast. I remapped parry to X because I couldn't hit the shoulder button as fast as the game wanted me to in many cases, and it was causing my RSI to flare up. The pinwheels are especially guilty of this.

-The animation lockout on your actions is both brutal and poorly telegraphed. I understand wanting to force players to choose when to attack, and to keep them from mindlessly mashing and cancelling into parry. But I think that would be better accomplished with a system that rewarded players for hitting opponents on-beat (or with a certain rhythm) instead.

-Most enemies have waaaaaaaaaaaay too much HP. My preference would be fewer hits that need to be timed to the beat or a specific rhythm. A lot of these enemies should not take as long to die as they do.

-There is no semblance of a difficulty curve. The first boss has syncopated rhythms and offbeats that shouldn't appear so early in the game; this is the attack pattern of a mid to late game boss, possibly a final boss depending on how hard you feel your game should be. That thing is a straight wall with no onboarding. Or perhaps this is the first boss on a harder difficulty mode—but not the default difficulty for new players. I could see this being the first boss's pattern on a hard or lunatic mode. 

The parry pinwheels also have outright bizarre rhythms and also ask you to parry miserably fast in some cases, right out the gate. A rhythm game note scroll, sheet music notation, -something-  to help with the bizarre rhythms would be welcome.

ALL THIS BEING SAID: I want to say that when it works, it's genuinely fun. I had fun beating the first boss once I learned it. I kind of want to go back and replay it, even now. But I was basically just brute forcing it the whole time and the learning process was miserable.


[b]Movement[/b]
===
It feels bad.

I hate to admit it, but it just doesn't feel good. The [spoiler]gravity beam[/spoiler] is clunky and the [spoiler]grappling hook[/spoiler] feels nigh uncontrollable. The jump feels kind of limp and never goes as far horizontally as I expect. Sprinting isn't a fun way to increase traversal speed. And I feel like your movement often interacts with gravity in... unexpected ways if you don't lock the gravity. Even then, I've had moments where I was... on a different gravity "plane" than I expected, and my movement turned out weird? Not sure how to really explain it.

Something here is just off on multiple levels.


[b]Puzzles[/b]
===
They're often just clunky. The gravity beam simply doesn't feel very good to use, and anything that wants you to cancel the beam and re-place it is an especially poor offender. Everything feels slow, and not particularly smooth either. Feedback is often kind of poor: it's sometimes unclear if you're doing the wrong thing or just doing the right thing incorrectly, especially on some more difficult puzzles. [spoiler]The puzzle for the hospital key is an especially bad offender here.[/spoiler]

I should say that I do like [spoiler]the way needle/thread tie things together, conceptually, even if it's really wonky in practice sometimes.[/spoiler]

=======================

One of the more frustrating gaming experiences I've had in awhile. I initially was drawn to this game when I heard it was similar to Gravity Rush, but with a Castlevania style or progression and a heavy emphasis on puzzle solving. The character design and visuals were very clearly inspired by Pseudoregalia, another game I enjoyed. Sounded promising enough, and I promise I tried my hardest to enjoy this game. I just can't do it. At best I can see myself giving it another try perhaps as it continues to give additional patches (assuming they iron out issues and increase accessibility), but I simply find the overall game loop incredibly miserable to say the least. In fact, it feels like every single aspect of this game was designed with at least a partial intent to annoy the player. 

For example, one of the basic things I would hope for in this subgenre of action adventure games is a decent map, and I certainly didn't get that. Just trying to make heads or tails of the map in this game is awful. The inventory system is awful. The controls feel terrible. The camera is absolutely horrendous and the game quite truly has built in stick drift. In fact the camera is so bad that the dev had to patch in basic deadzone stick fixing, but I'm still having horrendous stick drift that makes me never want to adjust the camera. 

Rather than try to double down on the gravity aspect of the game, combat is tied to...rhythm. I enjoy rhythm games and I like music. The soundtrack is fun, but the rhythm element is not. It is tacked on and not well explored. Most of the time, it is just a tedious novelty. At its worst, it is extremely obnoxious. The concept of rhythm based action has been done a lot better in recent times by other games, and I honestly don't think it was at all needed in this one. Instead it just poses as an additional barrier of annoyance for progression. 

Speaking of which, the real thing that glues it all together: progression. My time with Metro Gravity has more or less just been wandering around often upside down on the ceiling and who knows where. I'm just hoping to find something to do or somewhere to go. Just hoping to find purpose in this lonely world. On occasion I'll come across a puzzle. A lot of them leave me stumped. As an option they will sometimes leave a phone to help you. Supposedly the person on the phone should provide hints, but instead it is mostly just an opportunity for the dev to write snarky condescending text that is almost as much of a waste of time to read as the puzzle was to try to solve. I find most of the puzzles I get stuck on don't have this phone anyway, and the ones that aren't any more clear to me after I've been given the failed attempt at stand-up comedy. So it's just a lot of mindlessly trying out random things until something clicks, or doesn't. Worst case scenario is that it turns out I'm missing some random power or thing I need to progress. How was I supposed to know? Well I guess I wasn't. It's a lot of just banging the head on the wall, but with virtually no sense of tension or dynamics. The whole game is so sluggish and floaty, and getting around is very tedious because the travel points are awkwardly placed and the map is hardly any help at all. 

So in the end of the day, I found myself staring at the screen just asking why I was even bothering to try to force myself to like something I very clearly was having a miserable time playing. At the very least, I like the main character's design.
This game is cool but I'm starting to feel like this game is becoming more of a chore then an adventure after 5 hours in. Not sure I'll be able to finish it.

This game has really good ideas, almost none of them are executed well. It ends up being frustrating and the gravity mechanics will give you a headache.

The combat is not fun and is all about reflexes, asking you to press a single button to block most attacks the very instant you see a flashing circle. 

While some puzzles are very interesting most I've found in the few hours I've played have been platforming or reaction based, these are the two aspects where the game shows its flaws. 
Opening a door could be as simple as blocking an enemy bullet or as frustrating as fighting the gravity and hook controls for an hour. Time based trials (no timer, rather platforms disappearing in regular intervals) were not the way to go when even the slightest shift in topography will shake the camera and gravity.

The game sells itself as rhythm based, this mechanics is not executed well at all. Save from the boss fights its nowhere to be seen, it asks for memorization rather than feeling the beat, most of the time it makes no sense how its supposed to work.

My head is spinning, thank you very much.

3D plaformer were you control gravity

Metro Gravity is a rather interesting platformer were you can walk on anything and anywhere you go. Walls, ceilings, etc. Making it really fun to go through the levels and explore it at your own pace. It's awesome to know the dev was inspired by two great games like Pseudogralia and Super Mario Galaxy. Visually it looks amazing and the music goes great with the atmosphere and boss fights you do face along the way.

The game is fun sometimes and made with passion but there's some critiques i have for Metro Gravity.
The Camera: Walking on any surface is great but it can lead to some motion sickness. Thankfully i didn't but some puzzle platforming rooms, enemy encounters, and boss fights are infuriating cause the camera is CONSTANTLY going all over the place. Which is annoying cause i'm fighting with the camera rather than playing the game.
The Combat: Gameplay is mostly doing fun platforming but then there's the rather boring combat. It's a rhythmic hack n slash were all you do is parry, parry, parry and then hit once or twice while occasionally dodging and jumping to avoid enemy attacks. I have played Hi-Fi Rush and Metal Hellsinger which are great rhythm combat games and i know your suppose fight on beat with the music. It unfortunately isn't fun because enemies mostly can hit you from afar while you have to be closer to hit them and on top of that you do so low damage that it takes so long to kill some enemies it made me want to avoid the combat altogether cause it got really exhausting to fight anyone.
The Grappling Hook: This should have been a fun way to traverse the worlds but instead i fly into voids and lava to take damage, walls, ceilings, enemies who can hit you when your swinging around and i can't even reel into a spot without bumping into anything and slide on the ground. Worst is that when i have something behind my character and i wanna grapple something that's in front of me the game targets the one in the back because the targeting is garbage.
The Puzzles: Don't get me wrong some puzzles are fun and makes you think and utilize your items to be used. However there are some that makes you HATE puzzles cause they are poorly made. Pushing cubes are bad cause the momentum you give makes you do these annoying well timed gravity switching but it just flies somewhere else cause the gravity is fucked (even if you control it) and makes you start the process all over again. The Archive battery one is the worst and i thought this was great when i figured some solution. Until i looked online how to solve it and my god i was speechless of how utterly stupid this one was.

I was gonna talk about the story but i couldn't piece together what was going on. Except for the end which was alright but some scenes were really confusing.

It pains me to not recommend this game cause when i saw the inspiration from one of my childhood games and the trailer made me wanna buy it. But the negatives were way too much for me to have a constant rage inducing moments. But if you found some joy from this game that's great and i'm happy for you. That's what games should always be. FUN.

This is just my opinion so you can agree or disagree however you see Metro Gravity

5/10
